19yo F here, 60kg, 5'5'', very healthy, religious and virgin.

I have been researching the HPV gardasil shot and am really on the fence about whether to get it or not. My PCP and GYN are urging me to, saying I might get cancer and warts if I don't. I am very religious and am currently dating another virgin boy who I plan to marry soon and have children within 2-3 years, we are strictly monogamous. Adding this in because I think I'm at a much lower risk than most other 19 year-olds for that reason.

My doctors say now is the ideal time to get the shot but considering my low risk factor I want to know whether it is truly safe or not. My cousin actually developed GBS after the shot and almost died, luckily she did recover but it was a scare for the entire family and another reason why we've put it off. We thought maybe she was just a rare 1/1,000,000 event but then we started reading more and more stories.

I've read many many stories online in facebook groups and have seen movies about seriously scary adverse events including permanent arthritis, autoimmune conditions, paralysis, seizures, and chronic health issues. I've spoken to a few young women and mothers who say that their daughters are now disabled for years since the shot. Even a couple of my friends say they developed chronic fatigue or other weird health problems after. There seems to be something strange about this vaccine.

Are these stories real? What's happening? If the shot is so dangerous then why do doctors say it's safe and why do they continue to recommend it? 

I am not ethically or religiously opposed to the shot, I just don't know if it's worth it to me for the benefits vs. risks. The only chance I'd have of developing an HPV infection is if my husband cheated which I feel quite certain he won't, or if we were to divorce and date again later in life, but again I find that highly unlikely as we have a very stable relationship and are very committed. There is very little cancer in my family with the exception of my great uncle who smoked cigarettes and developed lung cancer. Besides that my family is very healthy, religious, monogamous, and long-lived (I understand this may not be relevant, but thought I would add this).

I made this account because I am very distressed about the decision and I want to know the truth, I want to know whether gardasil (hpv shot) is safe and whether these adverse events are truly connected to the shot. Thank you!
golden_answers: Honestly I have no idea why the uptake of HPV vaccine is so low. Rates of cervical cancer have dramatically fallen. You can't control what may happen in the future with your relationship. To me it is a no brainer. I will even be taking my son for it when he is old enough.

It only seems to work with actual fresh limes, not pre-processed bottled lime juice - you simply cut a wedge off and smear it liberally across your forehead and temples, and the pain usually recedes significantly within a minute. It also works just as well with frozen and re-thawed lime wedges, although the effect seems somewhat lessened if you heat them beyond room temperature when defrosting them.

Why would this be? What is it about lime juice that would just cure most headaches like magic within seconds?

My father, 59M, had a seizure today. He has no record or history of seizures, and has had no appetite and has been nauseous the last two weeks, losing 11lbs.
Today, he was throwing up all day, but seemed fine nonetheless. He was sitting down, and I saw him took off to the side, and his whole body started shaking. His muscles were stiff, he was drooling, and his lips were twitching. I tried to get him to respond but he wouldn’t. I immieditly called 911. He was shaking for around one minute, but he suddenly stood up and reached out for me, hitting my face. I ran outside because he seemed irrational. As I was outside, I saw him walk to the windows. He was scraping at the curtains, banging on the widow and running his hands on it. It didn’t look like he was necessarily trying to get my attention, his head and eyes were moving all around, and he seemed almost possessed. He then moved over to the glass front door and did the same thing. I saw him sit back down on the couch and a police officer arrived. He went to the door, and my dad answered. He seemed to be awake and was talking. The officer told him he had a seizure and he seemed extremely confused, like he had no memory of what happened and he was “fine.” The officer asked him some questions like what day it was, if he had any medicine, and he gave weird answers and seemed to be losing his balance. He was completely out of it. The ambulance took him to the hospital where he had another seizure, but they’re figuring things out from there. My only question is, is it normal for people to do that during/after a seizure? I told the officers and EMT’s what happened and they seemed confused. He looked almost possessed, and was going absolutely crazy. He’s never done anything like that. He has a history of anxiety and paranoia but not going crazy like that. Is it normal for people to be completely erratic after a seizure? I’m just really scared because it looked like something out of a horror movie.

Update: The hospital has done a lot of tests, but haven’t found much. They did find he had an irregular heart rhythm so he was transferred to cardiology. My mom visited him today, and he’s still very out of it. He isn’t remembering a lot and has ripped out his IV’s 4 times thinking he gets to go home soon. Unfortunately I’m not allowed to see him because I’m under 16, but I got to talk to him on the phone. He was nothing like himself, didn’t know what day it was or who his sisters name was. They’re going to do neurology tests tomorrow, so hopefully we’ll figure out what’s really wrong.
golden_answers: It is possible for people to display personality changes and act irrationally right after a seizure, pretty much everything is possible right after a seizure. Your pop needs a head MRI with contrast.

Spotlights of signal superintensity in the T2 and FLAIR sequences, in the perivencular white substance and semioval centers, which do not have an expansive, unspecific effect.

There is no evidence of an intraparenchymatous expansive process, extra-axial fluid collections, hypertensive ventriculomegaly, acute / sbuaguda intraparenchymal hemorrhage, deviation of midline structures or effacement of base cisterns

Usual flow at the level of the great intracranial arterial branches of the vertebro-basilar and carotid systems, according to Spin Echo criteria.

There is no area of ​​destruction to the free diffusion of water molecules evidenced by the sequence Echo Planar.

Diagnostic printing:

Signs of diffuse brain volume reduction, with compensatory ectasia of the supratentorial ventricular system, usual for the age group

Focuses of signal hyperintensity in the T2 and flair sequences in the supratentorial white matter, nonspecific, suggestive of gliosis resulting from microangiopathy.

​

​

So this exam was last year, go do a new one tomorrow and go back to the neurologist soon, is a bit hard to understand what that diagnosis mean, i just wanna to have more info to talk to the neurologist.
golden_answers:
TLDR: there are changes in the brain from long term blood vessel problems. This is not "normal" *per se* but is unfortunately very common, and these changes can in turn cause what is called **vascular dementia.** I think that this scan as written does not particularly rule in or rule out **Alzheimer's dementia** (it is also possible to have two causes of dementia). Either way, it still sounds like dementia.  


Neurologist is exactly the person to go see. Questions I would ask him/her: What is the cause of the memory loss and confusion? What should we do about it? They might say "I don't know the cause for sure," which is true, but it's OK to press them a little for an educated guess.  


# In detail

* Spotlights of signal superintensity...: Changes from blood vessel problems (like hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol). Some people might call these "mini strokes" but that term is used pretty loosely. When you see these spots on the MRI scan, the person may not have had any obvious stroke symptoms in the past (slurred speech, weakness, face drooping). These spots probably happened one or two at a time, over the course of years. Looks basically like [this picture.](  

* no evidence of an intraparenchymatous...: No sign of a cancer, no emergency situation with bleeding or fluid blockages (not surprising).  

* Usual flow...: This means they did a magnetic resonance *angiogram* in addition to the "regular" MRI. No blockages in the *large* blood vessels (which is good). But the small blood vessels are responsible for those T2 changes, as above.  

* No area of destruction... diffusion...: This means no stroke going on *right this moment*. Also good.  

* Signs of diffuse...: There is slightly less brain material there than there once was, and it seems to be affected all over (not in one particular place). This can go along with the problems with small blood vessels that we've been mentioning all along. *Sometimes* the radiologist will comment on areas that relate to Alzheimer's. The "classic" MRI of Alzheimer's shows volume reduction in specific parts of the brain (not diffuse) but this is honestly pretty tricky. "Diffuse" does not automatically mean "it's vascular dementia and not Alzheimer's." Personally I don't like the phrasing "usual for age group." Radiologists in the USA use it too. It may be "usual" to have an abnormal MRI, abnormal stress test of the heart, knee arthritis, glaucoma, etc. when you approach 80 years old, but too often this phrasing gets *misinterpreted* (by doctors, patients, and families alike) as "completely normal MRI which does not explain the patient's symptoms."   

* Focuses of signal hyperintensity...: They are just summarizing and restating what they said above.  


# Conclusion

I mostly focused on interpreting the MRI report, because that was the biggest part of your post. Obviously there's more to it (see caveats below). I'm sorry to hear that you father is having these memory problems.  


Classically, Alzheimer's dementia is a slow, steady loss of memory. But vascular dementia happens in sudden (but small) steps. Such as "I noticed in the middle of February that she kept asking the same question again. Then she stayed the same, but in November she started to forget what day it was." A lot of times, information from the family is *more important* than the MRI test in making the diagnosis. Your father is lucky to have you around helping him through this.  


# Caveats

I don't know 100% what you mean by "most of the exams." Probably you mean scans and lab tests, but I don't know if your father had neurocognitive testing (this is a process where you spend a long time with an examiner who asks memory questions, drawing tasks, planning tasks, etc.). I would be surprised if neurocognitive testing was normal given what you said.  


I also don't know exactly what you mean by "confusion." To doctors, there are ways to distinguish disorientation (like not knowing what day it is) from delirium (can be disoriented but also very much comes and goes, and involves problems with very short term attention tasks).

No matter what he eats or drinks at whatever time of day, he has a lot of upper GI gas that he has to force out. Stressful situations seem to be a significant trigger, but it happens even when he's calm. The real problem is at night when he's lying down and it builds up without him able to burp it up. About 45 min to an hour after he falls asleep, the pressure wakes him up in a panic because he can't breathe. He reports feeling very lightheaded and woozy during this time, and it's terrifying for me because he leaps up in the middle of the night sounding like he's having a panic attack: loudly gasping for air and shaking, clawing at his chest to breathe. The pressure has also started causing him pain in his chest.

He has seen four different GIs, a nutritionist, two chiropractors, and a couple GPs. He's had a barium swallow, an endoscopy, an acid reflux tube test, all of which showed normal results. He is currently waiting on the results from an immunolabs allergy test and a stool sample test for parasites. He's also getting a motility for GI tract sensitivities this week, but we aren't hopeful, considering every specialist just shrugs their shoulders without a clue.

Has anyone ever heard of this, or have ideas?

More specific info/history: No current medications, white, height 5'6", weight 175lb, previously smoked for 1 yr over 9 years ago. He rarely drinks alcohol. These symptoms manifested after he had a diaphragm pull for hiatal hernia in late 2010 to try and deal with massive acid-reflux. Her mother found her sluggish and hallucinating and brought her to the ER.  As of right now, the doctors are saying that her Tylenol level is 35, and she still isn't forming coherent sentences.  She's unable to recognize her parents.

  I wanted to ask here what we should be expecting.  My sister is distraught, and I want to give her the right information about what's going on, and how to help her friend while she's being treated.  I know that there are plans to send her to a psychiatric facility once her Tylenol level goes down, which is the only part I'm really familiar with.  I was 5150'd about 6 years ago for self-harm, but I was never hospitalized for any of my actual suicide attempts, so I'm in the dark right now.  Any information would be appreciated.  Thanks.
golden_answers:
What to expect is a question for the doctors involved.

Benadryl overdose can cause confusion and hallucinations, but care is mostly supportive until the Benadryl is metabolized away.

Tylenol overdose is extremely dangerous. Depending on the exact dose and how quickly treatment was initiated, she could be fine, but if the total amount was too high and not treated in time a Tylenol overdose can cause acute liver failure, which is very bad. If they're talking about transfer to a psychiatric facility then they're hopeful, at least.

Treatment in the facility you might also know. It's to have time to stabilize, talk with her about why she overdosed and come up with a plan of treatment to hopefully get her feeling a little better and critically to have support and a way to ask for help without putting her life at risk.

* Medications: None right now (but see list of meds already tried, below)
* Recreational: Alcohol (daily), marijuana (occasional), tobacco of any form (never), caffeine (daily)
* Diet: Ovo-lacto vegetarian diet for >40 years (mostly healthy foods)

**Problem Description**

For 3 years my dad has been suffering from painful nighttime gassiness (described as a dull pain, not sharp), which disturbs his sleep so much that he only gets a few hours of sleep per night. Pain lessens sometimes when gas moves. Not bothersome during the day. When passed, the gas is not the “methane” smelly type. Only pattern noticed is that it seems to get worse if rice or lentils are eaten. No complaints about stomach pain or heartburn. Normal daily bowel movements. ***Blastocystis hominis*** infection (overgrowth?) was/is the suspected reason for his problem (apparently this is a difficult bug to treat).

**Tests completed**

* Blood tests 2017: all normal except borderline elevated cholesterol
* CT scan 2017 – no additional abnormality (besides the diverticulosis)
* Stool tests, three since 2017, most recent in late 2018: All found “many” blastocystis hominis, no blood
* Colonoscopy 2009 – Diverticulosis, but PCP says average for his age (not bad), good lining, no mucus or bleeding

**PCP treatments attempted** (no change to symptoms)

* Metronidazole (two rounds)
* Paromomycin
* Nitazoxanide (two rounds)

**Behavior/dietary changes attempted**

* Simeticone – no change
* No beer/alcohol for 1 week (tried two separate times) – no change
* Probiotics – s. boulardii (tried one 5 billion capsule 2x/day for one week) – had a slight bad reaction: upset stomach
* Continues to avoid rice and lentils – problem remains but is at least not exacerbated

**Potential ideas we read about but he has not yet tried**

* Fasting for 2 days and then slowly adding foods back in (this is PCP’s current recommended next step)
* TMP-SMX
* Fecal transplant
* Garlic, ginger, cloves
* Gluten-free
* Dairy-free
* Avoiding fiber
* Ordering more comprehensive stool analysis (we saw online that Great Plains Laboratory and Genova Diagnostics have what look like much more detailed results than the stool tests he's already had, but they both have horrible reviews for billing problems... unsure about them)

**Current status and questions**

PCP conferred with an Infectious Disease doctor and they are now saying this blastocystis should have resolved itself on its own if my dad didn’t have some other underlying problem. Should he be looking at IBS, Celiac, Crohn’s? Something else? Should he request a particular type of specialist/test/treatment? Do any of our potential ideas look particularly good or bad? Would it be worth it for him to request sleep medications in the meantime, until the underlying problem is (hopefully) resolved?

Many thanks in advance for your time. Happy to answer questions.

**CBC w/diff / CMP / Lipase / Amylase**

About me: 34F, 185lbs, 5’4”, white. 

I was diagnosed with chlamydia a few weeks back. I was prescribed 1g of azithromycin, which came as a powder to mix in water. I failed to take the whole dose at once as instructed. I realized I had missed pouring about a quarter of it into my water, and then I did end up taking the rest about 12 hours later. That was on May 4th or so. 

The only symptom I had ever noticed was just daily cervical mucus / vaginal discharge that didn’t seem abnormal but was more copious than usual. That mostly dried up about a week after I took the medicine. 

But for the past week I’ve still noticed some kind of gummy discharge first thing in the morning. And a couple days ago, it looked like some brown spotting. Yesterday it looked sort of pinkish/yellowish. I thought maybe my period was about to start. 

But today it looked mostly a yellowish color when I wiped. I only noticed it first thing in the morning and not since then. 

I’m worried the azithromycin didn’t treat the chlamydia, but I don’t know if I’m just reading too much into the mucus/discharge. It doesn’t seem abnormal except that I wouldn’t really expect to see any mucus right now in my cycle, and it is a different color than usual.

Should I get retested for chlamydia? How soon would it show up again if the antibiotic is now longer in my system? I don’t want it to lead to any complications but I also don’t want to retest too soon and get a false negative. Am I overreacting to the symptoms? I don’t notice anything out of the normal other than the slightly unusual mucus/discharge. 

Any advice would be appreciated.
golden_answers:
I typically recommend retesting at 6-12 weeks anyway (for people that take the usual dose it is to test for re-infection). 

Call your provider. If my patient told me this story, I would just retreat because the azithromycin is so low risk and has minimal side effects. Maybe not what every doctor would do, but that’s my practice whenever a patient is concerned about getting the whole dose. You can also get treated in pill form if that is easier. 

Also, make sure your partner was treated if you are still involved. Make sure all partners are treated. In non-monogamous couples I also treat female partners. The most common reason that a woman has persistent chlamydia infection is because she was re-infected by a partner that wasn’t treated. Many states in the US allow the gynecologist to send medication for “expedited partner treatment” as well. 

Chlamydia is very very common, and rarely causes complications. It is usually asymptomatic.

Edit: Also, use condoms until you speak with your gynecologist. I typically recommend condoms for two weeks after treatment, unless an atypical situation like being unsure about treatment.

I know there are a few neurologists that frequent r/askdocs so I thought this would be a shot. I'm not looking for a diagnosis, just have a few questions.

**Back story**

My brother, 46 athletic male, was in a rollover ATV/4Wheeler accident 15 days ago. He was riding down a country road adjacent to his ranch and rolled with a 650-pound ATV causing both cranial/facial crushing and accelerate/decelerate brain injuries. He was helicoptered to a Level 1 Trauma Hospital specializing in Brain and Spine injuries. While he raced competitive motocross for most of his life, he was not wearing a helmet at the time of the accident as he was 2 minutes from his ranch tending to a stuck vehicle. He was breathing on his own at the time of the accident but has not been conscious or significantly responsive since the accident. It happened in front of his wife so she was able to tend to him immediately and call for help. He was breathing but hypoxic injuries were a concern.

Within 24 hours he was placed into a medically induced (pentobarbital) coma and given a GCS of 3. CT Scans showed 17 cranial fractures along with a brain hemorrhage on the left side. Hypoxic injuries and Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) were the two other things we were not able to confirm but were on the list of concerns of possible injury to the frontal cortex. We knew we would be able to discover these based on an MRI if we could get him stable enough to complete an MRI. After 5 days, coma medication was weened off but Intra-cranial pressure began to spike (ICP as high as 48 for a few minutes) so he was placed back on the pentobarbital for 2 more days. On day 7 of the medically induced coma, he was weened once again off the medication and evaluated every 12 hours. He’s been unresponsive to name calls and noxious pressure to the sternum other than some arm and leg twitches and recently eye fluttering (not opening but eye lid movement). Eyes are fixed and do not respond to light. He coughs, involuntarily, based on ventilator tube changes and suction. His lower body is abnormally postured with stiff legs and pointed toes. Hands are tight, but not so much clinched (based on the research on Decerebrate Posturing). His head is not tilted back. We’ve been here for 5 days now and he was stable enough to get an MRI as his ICP levels have been between 9 and 20. He's currently at a GCS of 4 and has been off everything for nearly a week other than Oxycodine for pain. This sounds crazy but to get a good exam and response, his team wanted him off as much as possible to get an accurate assessment of cognition.

**Here are the impression notes from the CT Scan:**

The right frontal approach ventriculostomy catheter now terminates left of midline, at the junction of the left lateral ventricle/ foramen of Monroe. A small amount of intraventicular hemorrhage on the right has increased since the prior study, likely related to the catheter placement.

There is no hydrocephalus or midline shift.

The intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the left basal ganglia, and adjacent vasogenic edema, are unchanged.

A small chronic infarct of the left caudate nucleus is redemonstrated.

The small amount of intraventricular hemorrhage, in the posterior portions of the lateral ventricles, has diminished in quantity.

**Here are the impression notes from the MRI:**

Persistent right parietal ventriculostomy catheter, with tip adjacent to septum pellucideum. Persistent nonspecific edema and hemorrhagic blood products surrounding the catherter tract.

Persistent focal hemorrhage and edema in the left inferior basal ganglia.

Few additional tiny regions of the susceptibility artifact are also noted in the high right cerebral convexity, and the medial right thalamus.

Additional tiny intra-ventricular hemorrhages in the occipital horns and both lateral ventricles.

I’ve posted his MRI here [ (the first few seconds are still and he does have a PICC line)

**My questions**

Based on what we’ve been told, he’s been diagnosed with Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) Grade 3 in both the frontal cortex, occipital horns, and the brain stem. They’re not seeing anything that would indicate hypoxic injuries but with a DAI Grade 3, it’s pretty much worst case scenario with or without Hypoxic injury. With that said, does the MRI correspond with these injuries? Based on other imaging I've looked at of DAI Grade 3, I'm not seeing as much "black dots" of injury but that could be from swelling. Is there anything else that I should ask about my brother’s condition as we try to figure out what’s best for him and his family?

Thank you for reading and God bless.

**EDIT:** I just want to give a quick update. After reviewing many of the things that you all gave us guidance on and consulting with his medical team, we made the family decision to seek hospice care. We were concerned that he was breathing over the ventilator so we were unsure of what the next few days would hold and he moved on to the next world just a few minutes later. His body was just unable to recover. He went peacefully without issue.

I want thank you all for your kindness, guidance and support during this post. The world is still a bright and loving place and from my family to yours, I wish you nothing but health, safety and happiness in your future.  


I am leaving this post up to hopefully give someone in the future some answers that may help them on their journey.

So on Friday I (26M) got my second Moderna shot and was feeling pretty good afterwards. Then about 18 hours after, I started to develop some pretty hard side effects. Headache, bodyache, fever and chills. If I had my blanket on I was so hot I was sweating, but if I had it off I felt like I was in the middle of the South Pole.

But all of those are routine side effects of the vaccine (not so sure of the severity, but they’re listed on the CDC and FDA websites as what to expect).

What bothers me though is that my heart rate was extremely elevated and so was my blood pressure. My normal resting heart rate is about 55 (I’m fairly active and healthy) but for hours my heart rate was about 95 even though I was completely resting. I could also tell my blood pressure was higher as I could feel my heart pounding (similar to how it feels to get a good workout, not extreme but noticeable).

What bothers me is I was unable to find anywhere that said that this was a normal side effect of getting the vaccine. I’m well aware of the risk of heart inflammation and this is one of the symptoms of that. And considering I’m in the prime demographic for that adverse side effect, this worries me.

The other two symptoms are shortness of breath (I didn’t have any, but that’s only listed as happening to half of patients) and chest pain (I did have chest discomfort, but nothing I would define as chest pain. It was in the center of my chest so could have been a mix of what I ate and muscle aches).

I slept it off and felt completely fine the next day, 36 hours after getting the shot. But this bothers me if I had slight heart inflammation, as I know it’s practically a death sentence (medication for life and >50% mortality rate 4 years after diagnoses).

So as I’m really worried about my health, is what I experienced normal or acceptable?
golden_answers:
An elevated heart rate is normal - it's just another sign that your immune system is active. Elevated heart rate is also normal when you have a fever.

No evidence here that you had anything like myocarditis, and it's absolutely not a death sentence. Most people who have developed myocarditis related to the COVID-19 vaccine are better in a week or two.

It’s ruined my most important development years, I’ve never had a girlfriend, lost all my mates and I’ve tried everything. 

The worst thing I find about this condition is there is no break. Once the skin has painfully peeled off, it’s raw, hurts and within 12 hours I can feel the buildup coming. It’s constant and it’s right slap on the centre of my face, the worst place it could be. I’m really exhausted and have tried so so so many things, it’s my life’s focus, there hasn’t been a day in the last 5 years where I haven’t researched what I can do. 

As well as the peeling, my lips get inflamed and have a sort of red border around them after eating most foods, laughing and also after climaxing. It makes my look like a literal clown. I don’t eat out any more. This made me think it was histamine in the food I was eating but I’ve kinda ruled that out now. My theories are: leaky gut… mast cell activation syndrome….or some sort of hormone issue. I’ve been send all round the country to different doctors, with no success. So I’m old (40) and I can’t figure out how to link my old post, but here goes. I was having stomach and abdominal pain so bad that I didn’t want to be here anymore. Well I was at a wedding this weekend, and I got out of the limousine and fell on my knees. My legs just gave out. I was tired but nothing out of the ordinary. (This is important later.) I went through the weekend and was at work Monday when I started to feel nauseous. I went another two hours feeling dizzy and nauseous and having severe heart palpitations. I keep going for another 20 mins until I start seeing black and white spots. I know if I stay I’m gonna pass out and they won’t find me, so I run to my bosses office and tell her I need to go to the hospital now. She sits me down and the school nurse comes and takes my pulse (99) and calls my husband. 

I go to urgent care, who throws me into a wheel chair and after triage tells me I need to go to the ED right now. I go, they get me in ASAP and hook me up to heart monitors. Nurse comes in and draws blood. They tell me I’m staying for a few hours to get a second blood draw in two hours. Doc comes in abs tells me that I my potassium levels are super low (2.6) and that I have to have an IV with some potassium in it. Cool. I’m okay with that. Apparently low potassium levels can cause your heart to stop, and also cause your stomach to stop working, which causes pain as well as explain why my legs have given out and my weird leg cramping and fire like lava going through my legs, as well as having absolutely ZERO energy. I have been dealing with palpitations for a year, but I also have anxiety so it was impossible to know what was causing it all this time. 

I’ll tell you, I felt like super woman after they gave me that IV. I can’t believe I lived this way so long when this was what I needed. My heart stopped fluttering but I do still have a few light palpitations and some dizziness. I can actually have a bowel movement and I don’t stay full on one meal a day. It always felt like food just sat in my stomach forever. I am getting a holter monitor for 5 days, and my potassium levels checked again in two weeks. 

I’m hoping this is the answer for me. Either way, I can verify my pain is lots lower, as well as my energy levels higher which improves my quality of life drastically. If all I need addressed is my abdominal pain and I have the energy to do my job and keep food on the table, then I am a happy lady. 

I still have an appointment with my GP in less than two weeks to address pain relief. I thought I’d share an update. 

PS my old blood work did show I was low, but not this low. It ranged between 2.9-3.0 the last two tests before this one.

Patient: male, 23, undergoing treatment for SMA, no comorbidities

Treatment is intrathecal injections. He always has a spinal headache post injection for several days before his doctor recommends going to the ER for a blood patch. They’ve switched to a sprotte needle, that didn’t help. Last spinal headache lasted longer that 2 weeks. Patient is high functioning and missing work/school. This has happened 6 times. 


For someone with SMA, lying flat for that long can lead to muscle loss which is devastating. 

Is it possible to do a prophylactic blood patch at the time of intrathecal injection?  Would this be reasonable to request?  Any other advice is appreciated. Main concern is muscle loss from extended bed rest.
golden_answers:
What gauge spinal needle are they using? Hopefully 27g if possible. It seems crazy that he would have a post dural puncture headache (PDPH) from such a small puncture site, but not unheard of. 

I would not recommend a prophylactic epidural blood patch (EBP) at the time of intrathecal injection. Conservative recommendations say to wait 24 hours after dural puncture before attempting EBP to relieve PDPH. At my facility, we will start thinking about EBP at around hour 12 if we’ve tried all the conservative treatments (sumatriptan, caffeine, hydration), but we still typically wait the 24 hours. 

Another option to treat PDPH is called a sphenopalatine ganglion (SPG) block. [Article here.]( While it’s less invasive than an EBP, it’s a bit more time consuming. I’ve had lots of success with them. I use 3cc total (1.5cc each side) of 4% lidocaine on the long wooden handled cotton tips, incrementally dosing by dropping down the handle and leaving them in place 20 min. An SPG block would be my first suggestion for his next PDPH! It’s a very low risk, high reward procedure. And if it doesn’t work, he can always try a second SPG block or go to an EBP if desired.

results.question: WHAT exercises can I do, safely, with asthma?
golden_answers:
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB), also called exercise-induced asthma, is a narrowing of the airways in the lungs that is triggered by physical activity.

					EIB is common in patients with chronic asthma, who frequently experience flare-ups while exercising. But it can also occur in otherwise healthy individuals who experience asthma symptoms only when they exercise.

					Symptoms of Exercise-Induced Asthma
					If you have EIB, you may have problems breathing within five to 20 minutes after exercise. Symptoms of EIB are similar to those of chronic asthma, but the timing of the symptoms is closely linked with physical activity.

					Your symptoms may include:
					* Wheezing
					* Tight chest
					* Cough
					* Shortness of breath
					* Chest pain (rarely)

					Triggers
					People with EIB are typically very sensitive to both low temperatures and dry air. Air is usually warmed and humidified by the nose, but during demanding activity people breathe more through their mouths. This allows cold, dry air to reach your lower airways and your lungs without passing through
					your nose, triggering asthma symptoms.

					Air pollutants, high pollen levels and viral respiratory infections may also be triggers. Other causes of symptoms while exercising include being out of shape, poorly controlled nasal allergies or vocal cord issues.
					Even the sport you choose can affect your symptoms. Swimming is considered less likely to cause asthma symptoms because the warm, humid environment of the pool does not aggravate the airways. Warm-weather activities and those requiring only short bursts of energy are also recommended. These
					include:
					* Hiking
					* Baseball
					* Golf
					* Walking
					* Leisure biking

					Because cold, dry air can make symptoms worse, as can activities that require continuous exertion, it is recommended that individuals with EIB avoid sports like:
					* Cross-country skiing

					* Hockey
